title: Finite differentiability of kernels of sufficiently negative local symbols
statement: Use $\mathbf R,\mathbf C$ [def-weil-field]. Fix integers $m\geq1$, $p,q,k\geq0$ and $r<-m-k$, and an open set $U\subseteq\mathbf R^m$. Let $a:U\times\mathbf R^m\to\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(\mathbf C^p,\mathbf C^q)$ be a symbol of order $r$ with the derivative estimates of [def-sfb-symbol-pseudodifferential-operators]. Let $\chi,\psi$ be smooth real functions on $U$ whose supports are compact subsets of $U$. For $x,y\in U$, set $$H(x,y)=\chi(x)\psi(y)(2\pi)^{-m}\int_{\mathbf R^m}e^{i(x-y)\cdot\xi}a(x,\xi)\,d\xi,$$ and extend $H$ by zero to $\mathbf R^m\times\mathbf R^m$. This is an absolutely convergent matrix integral and $H$ is $C^k$, with support contained in $\operatorname{supp}\chi\times\operatorname{supp}\psi$. Its partial derivatives of total order at most $k$ are obtained by differentiating the integrand, including both spatial cutoffs; the corresponding integrals converge absolutely and locally uniformly in $(x,y)$. More precisely, for any fixed smooth compactly supported frequency cutoff $\rho$ equal to one near zero, replacing $a(x,\xi)$ by $a(x,\xi)\rho(\xi/R)$ gives kernels tending to $H$ with all those derivatives locally uniformly as $R\to\infty$. For every smooth compactly supported $f:\mathbf R^m\to\mathbf C^p$, the localized oscillatory quantization of the cited definition satisfies $$\chi\operatorname{Op}(a)(\psi f)(x)=\int_{\mathbf R^m}H(x,y)f(y)\,dy.$$ The right side is a $C^k$ function of $x$ and represents the same distribution. Its derivatives through order $k$ are the integrals with $\partial_x^\alpha H$. For real-valued $f$, replacing the left side by $\chi\operatorname{Re}\operatorname{Op}(a)(\psi f)$ and $H$ by $\operatorname{Re}H$ gives the corresponding real matrix formula.

source.place: Demailly, Differential and pseudodifferential operators on manifolds, §3, (3.3)–(3.5), Schwartz kernel (3.8)–(3.9), pp.6–8, and regularizing operators (3.12), pp.9–10. WANTED locally; read online https://www-fourier.univ-grenoble-alpes.fr/~demailly/analytic_geometry_2019/pseudodiff.pdf. Finite differentiability version of the Fourier-kernel argument, with the 1/(2π)^m convention of def-sfb-symbol-pseudodifferential-operators.

proof.text: Write $z=(x,y)$ and $c=(2\pi)^{-m}$. On $U\times U$ put $B(z,\xi)=c\chi(x)\psi(y)e^{i(x-y)\cdot\xi}a(x,\xi)$, and put $B=0$ elsewhere. For each fixed $\xi$, this is smooth on all of $\mathbf R^{2m}$: outside the compact sets $K=\operatorname{supp}\chi\subset U$ and $L=\operatorname{supp}\psi\subset U$ it is locally zero, including at the boundary of $U$. If either support is empty the conclusion is immediate, so assume both nonempty. The same zero-extension argument applies to each spatial derivative. Every derivative of either cutoff is bounded: apply [lem-sfb-compact-real-function-minimum] to the negative of its absolute value on its compact support (or on $K$ or $L$). Symbol estimates on $K$ are those of [def-sfb-symbol-pseudodifferential-operators].

source.place: Demailly, Differential and pseudodifferential operators on manifolds, §3 (3.3)–(3.5), pp.6–7, (3.8)–(3.9), p.8, and (3.12), pp.9–10; finite-order version supplied by Q145, with the item's Fourier normalization. Online PDF read; locally WANTED.

proof.text:
The Leibniz rule gives an explicit finite sum for $\partial_x^\alpha\partial_y^\beta B$. Index its terms by $\alpha_1+\alpha_2+\alpha_3=\alpha$ and $\beta_1+\beta_2=\beta$; a term, apart from the multinomial coefficients and $c$, is
$$ (\partial^{\alpha_1}\chi)(x)(\partial^{\beta_1}\psi)(y)e^{i(x-y)\cdot\xi}(i\xi)^{\alpha_2}(-i\xi)^{\beta_2}\partial_x^{\alpha_3}a(x,\xi). $$
Thus for $|\alpha|+|\beta|=j\leq k$ its norm is at most $C_{\alpha\beta}(1+|\xi|)^{r+j}$, uniformly in $z$; the constants use only the cutoff bounds of step 1 and finitely many symbol estimates with frequency derivative zero. Since $r+j\leq r+k<0$ and $1+t\geq\sqrt{1+t^2}$ for $t\geq0$, this is at most $C_{\alpha\beta}w(\xi)$, where $w(\xi)=(1+|\xi|^2)^{(r+k)/2}$. The identical bounds for full Frechet derivatives $D_z^jB$ follow by writing their finitely many coordinate entries and summing their absolute values. All these functions are Borel measurable (they are smooth).

source.place: Demailly, Differential and pseudodifferential operators on manifolds, §3 (3.3)–(3.5), pp.6–7, (3.8)–(3.9), p.8, and (3.12), pp.9–10; finite-order version supplied by Q145, with the item's Fourier normalization. Online PDF read; locally WANTED.

proof.text: Take $s=-(r+k)/2>m/2$. By [lem-sfb-euclidean-bracket-integrable], $w=(1+|\xi|^2)^{-s}$ is integrable. The majorant criterion in [lem-sfb-vector-integral-majorant-linearity] therefore makes every integral of $D_z^jB$ ($0\leq j\leq k$) absolutely convergent. Here matrices and multilinear maps on finite-dimensional spaces are complete, and complex vector spaces may be regarded as real Banach spaces. Define $I_j(z)=\int D_z^jB(z,\xi)\,d\xi$. For any sequence $z_n\to z$, the integrands converge pointwise and are bounded by $C_jw$; [lem-sfb-oscillatory-cutoff-convergence] shows $I_j(z_n)\to I_j(z)$. Thus each $I_j$ is continuous, also across the zero-extension boundary. Apply [lem-sfb-dominated-integral-frechet-derivative] to $F=D_z^jB$ for $j<k$: its derivative is $D_z^{j+1}B$, bounded by $C_{j+1}w$ on the entire parameter neighbourhood, and all required measurability and initial integrability hypotheses have just been verified. Starting with $H=I_0$, induction gives $D^jH=I_j$ for $j\leq k$. This proves $C^k$ regularity and the stated partial-derivative formulas. Since $B$ vanishes outside $K\times L$, so does $H$.

source.place: Demailly, Differential and pseudodifferential operators on manifolds, §3 (3.3)–(3.5), pp.6–7, (3.8)–(3.9), p.8, and (3.12), pp.9–10; finite-order version supplied by Q145, with the item's Fourier normalization. Online PDF read; locally WANTED.

proof.text:
Let $\rho_R(\xi)=\rho(\xi/R)$, $R>0$, and $M=\sup|\rho|<\infty$, using [lem-sfb-compact-real-function-minimum] on the negative of $|\rho|$ on its compact support. Spatial differentiation never differentiates $\rho_R$. The argument of step 3 therefore gives $D^jH_R=\int\rho_R D_z^jB$ for $j\leq k$, since $|\rho_R|\leq M$. Integral linearity and the majorant estimate of [lem-sfb-vector-integral-majorant-linearity] imply
$$\sup_z\|D^jH_R(z)-D^jH(z)\|\leq C_j\int |\rho(\xi/R)-1|w(\xi)\,d\xi.$$
The scalar integrand tends to zero pointwise and is bounded by $(M+1)w$. Apply [lem-sfb-oscillatory-cutoff-convergence] to the filter $R\to+\infty$ to see that the bound tends to zero. This proves even global uniform convergence of all asserted derivatives. Absolute convergence is also uniform in the usual frequency-tail sense: apply the same dominated convergence node to $w(\xi)\mathbf1_{|\xi|>T}$ as $T\to\infty$ and bound every derivative tail by $C_j\int_{|\xi|>T}w$. In particular the required locally uniform absolute convergence holds.

source.place: Demailly, Differential and pseudodifferential operators on manifolds, §3 (3.3)–(3.5), pp.6–7, (3.8)–(3.9), p.8, and (3.12), pp.9–10; finite-order version supplied by Q145, with the item's Fourier normalization. Online PDF read; locally WANTED.

proof.text: For the given test vector $f$, the scalar function $h(y)=\|f(y)\|$ is continuous and compactly supported, so [lem-sfb-continuous-compact-support-integrable] applied to $h$ regarded as complex-valued gives $\int h<\infty$. For fixed $x$, $\|B(x,y,\xi)f(y)\|\leq C_0 w(\xi)h(y)$. This is a product of integrable factors. More explicitly, integrate its norm in $\xi$ first using [lem-sfb-vector-integral-majorant-linearity]; the result is bounded by $C_0(\int w)h(y)$ and hence integrable. The product criterion and Fubini equality of [lem-sfb-product-fubini-integral-swap] now apply to the Borel function $(y,\xi)\mapsto B(x,y,\xi)f(y)$, and also to $\rho_RBf$. Lebesgue measures are sigma-finite and the finite-dimensional vector target is a real Banach space. Consequently the cutoff quantization $T_Rf$ is exactly $\int H_R(x,y)f(y)\,dy$, with no conditionally convergent interchange.

source.place: Demailly, Differential and pseudodifferential operators on manifolds, §3 (3.3)–(3.5), pp.6–7, (3.8)–(3.9), p.8, and (3.12), pp.9–10; finite-order version supplied by Q145, with the item's Fourier normalization. Online PDF read; locally WANTED.

proof.text: Step 4 and the integral norm estimate give $\sup_x\|T_Rf(x)-G(x)\|\leq\sup_{x,y}\|H_R-H\|\int h\to0$, where $G(x)=\int H(x,y)f(y)\,dy$. Pairing with any compactly supported smooth dual test $v$ gives a bound by this supremum times $\int\|v\|$, which is finite by [lem-sfb-continuous-compact-support-integrable] applied to its continuous compactly supported norm. Thus the distributional limit defining the localized $\chi\operatorname{Op}(a)(\psi f)$ in [def-sfb-symbol-pseudodifferential-operators] is the distribution represented by $G$. This identifies the oscillatory action with the displayed absolutely convergent kernel integral. It also proves cutoff independence in this range of orders.

source.place: Demailly, Differential and pseudodifferential operators on manifolds, §3 (3.3)–(3.5), pp.6–7, (3.8)–(3.9), p.8, and (3.12), pp.9–10; finite-order version supplied by Q145, with the item's Fourier normalization. Online PDF read; locally WANTED.

proof.text: For $0\leq j\leq k$, set $J_j(x)=\int D_x^jH(x,y)f(y)\,dy$. Step 3 and the integral bound give $\|D_x^jH(x,y)f(y)\|\leq C_j(\int w)h(y)$ uniformly in $x,y$. These are integrable majorants. Dominated convergence [lem-sfb-oscillatory-cutoff-convergence] makes each $J_j$ continuous, and [lem-sfb-dominated-integral-frechet-derivative] applied for $j<k$ gives $DJ_j=J_{j+1}$. The hypotheses hold because $H$ is $C^k$, the integrands are continuous in $y$, and the derivative bound holds on a full neighbourhood. Hence $G=J_0$ is $C^k$ with the claimed derivatives. Finally all finite-dimensional integrals can be taken coordinatewise. For real $f$, the equality $\operatorname{Re}(Hf)=(\operatorname{Re}H)f$ and real linearity of integration give the last formula, and the same derivative formulas pass to the real coordinates. If $p=0$ or $q=0$ all matrices or outputs are zero, so the same assertions hold.
